mainTopic: The number of judges for money cases: the sources for three, whether a court must be odd-numbered, and רבי's five
overview: The amud opens with the end of an answer: the משנה lists חצי נזק, and then full נזק, because of how it was already listing other payments. The גמרא then asks where we learn that money cases need three judges. רבי יאשיה counts three mentions of the word אלהים in the פסוקים. רבי יונתן does not count the first mention, so he counts two and adds a third because a בית דין cannot be even-numbered. The גמרא shows that both agree first mentions are not normally counted. רבי יאשיה counts this one only because the תורה chose the word אלהים over 'the judge'. The גמרא then explains that רבי יאשיה, like and even beyond רבי יהודה, allows an even-numbered court. He applies the odd-number rule only to capital cases, but still learns majority rule for money cases through a קל וחומר. Finally, a ברייתא brings רבי's view that money cases need five judges. רבי אבהו knocks out the first explanation for this, and the גמרא gives a new source: 2 + 2 from the פסוקים, plus 1 so the court is not even.

steps.title: Why the משנה also lists half damage and full damage
steps.stepSummary: This is the end of an answer. Once the משנה listed payments that do not match the actual loss, it also listed חצי נזק, which is also not equal to the loss. Because it listed חצי נזק, it also listed full נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: …is money that is not paid according to its actual value, so the משנה also taught half damage, which is also money not paid according to its value. And since it needed to teach half damage, it also taught full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer that started on the previous page. It explains why the משנה bothers to mention חצי נזק and נזק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chain goes like this. Some payments are more than the loss, so the משנה lists them. חצי נזק belongs in the same group because it is less than the loss, so it is listed too. Full נזק is listed only to round out the list next to חצי נזק.

keyTerms.meaning: Paid according to the actual value of the loss, no more and no less
Since; because (it was already teaching something else)

phrases.english: …is money that is not paid according to its value,
phrases.notes: This line continues from the previous daf. It means payments that are more than the actual loss.

phrases.english: so he also taught half damage,
since that too is money not paid according to its value.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַיְּידֵי דְּקָא בָּעֵי לְמִיתְנֵא חֲצִי נֵזֶק,
phrases.english: And since he needed to teach half damage,
he also taught full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַיְּידֵי דְּקָא בָּעֵי לְמִיתְנֵא חֲצִי נֵזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes an answer from the previous page about the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a listing in the משנה by how it fits with the items around it
steps.terutzMaskana: חצי נזק is listed because, like the other payments, it does not equal the loss. Full נזק is listed only to go along with חצי נזק.
steps.whatToRemember: Sometimes the משנה includes an item only because it naturally goes along with something else it already listed (אַיְּידֵי).

steps.title: Where do we learn the need for three judges?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source in the תורה that money cases need a בית דין of three.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three judges: from where do we learn this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It asks where the requirement of three judges comes from, and this sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stated that these cases are judged by three. Now the גמרא wants to find that number in the פסוקים themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: Three: from where do we derive it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after finishing the discussion of the list
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the פסוקים for having three judges

steps.title: רבי יאשיה counts three mentions of אלהים
steps.stepSummary: The word אלהים, meaning judges or court, appears three times in the פסוקים about a guardian accused of theft. רבי יאשיה says each mention stands for one judge, so the total is three.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'The owner of the house shall come near to the court (אלהים)': that is one. 'The case of both of them shall come before the court (אלהים)': that is two. 'Whom the court (אלהים) condemns': that is three. These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. רבי יאשיה counts each appearance of the word אלהים as one judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these פסוקים, אלהים means judges, not God. Three appearances of the word give three judges. Notice that he counts the very first mention too.

keyTerms.meaning: Here it means judges or a court
The owner of the house (here, the guardian holding the item)

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
“The owner of the house shall come near to the court,”
phrases.notes: שמות 22:7

phrases.english: here is one;
“The case of both of them shall come before the court,”
phrases.notes: שמות 22:8

phrases.english: here are two;
“Whom the court shall condemn,”
here are three.
These are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Three mentions of אלהים give three judges
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each mention of אלהים counts as one judge, including the first

steps.title: רבי יונתן: the first mention does not count, so add one
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן says the first mention of אלהים is needed to teach the basic law, so it cannot be counted. He counts only two mentions. Since a בית דין cannot have an even number, one more judge is added, making three.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: The first mention was said first, to teach the basic law, and we do not learn from first mentions. Rather, 'the case of both of them shall come before the court' is one, and 'whom the court condemns' is two. A court cannot be evenly split, so we add one more to them, and that makes three.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן reaches the same number, three, but in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He rejects counting the first mention because it is needed just to tell us to go to court at all. That leaves two judges from the פסוקים. A third is added by reasoning, because an even number of judges could end in a tie.

keyTerms.meaning: First mentions of a word in a passage
We do not expound or learn from it
A court with an even number of judges, which could tie

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
The first one was stated first,
phrases.notes: He means the first mention is needed just to teach the basic law, so it is not free to be counted.

phrases.english: and we do not expound first mentions.
Rather, “The case of both of them shall come before the court”
here is one;
“Whom the court shall condemn”
here are two;
and a court may not be even-numbered.
So we add one more to them,
and here are three.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר רִאשׁוֹן תְּחִילָּה נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes how רבי יאשיה counted, but reaches the same number
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two judges come from the פסוקים, and a third is added so the court is not even-numbered
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יונתן does not disagree that a בית דין has three judges. He only disagrees about how we learn it.

steps.title: Do they argue about counting first mentions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument is a general one: רבי יאשיה counts first mentions, and רבי יונתן does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about whether we expound first mentions? One master holds we do, and the other master holds we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a general principle behind the argument. It is setting up the next step, which will test this idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this suggestion were true, the dispute would be about a broad rule for reading the תורה, not just these פסוקים. The גמרא raises the idea so that it can check it.

phrases.english: Shall we say they argue about whether we expound first mentions?
One master holds: we expound first mentions,
and the other master holds: we do not expound first mentions.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for the principle behind the dispute in steps 3 and 4
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute is about the general rule of דורשין תחילות

steps.title: Everyone agrees, but the unusual word אלהים makes it countable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone agrees that first mentions are not normally counted. רבי יאשיה counts this one only because the תורה could have said 'the judge' and chose אלהים instead, which shows it is meant to be counted.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees we do not expound first mentions. רבי יאשיה could tell you: if so, let the פסוק say 'the owner of the house shall come near to the judge.' Why does it say 'to the court (אלהים)'? Learn from this that it is meant for the count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion. It shows that the two do not disagree about the general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a first mention is needed for the basic law, so it is not counted. Here, though, the basic law could have been taught with the plain word שופט. Choosing the word אלהים instead signals that this mention also joins the count.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (explaining a position)

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees that
we do not expound first mentions.
Rabbi Yoshiya could say to you:
If so, let the verse say:
“The owner of the house shall come near to the judge.”
phrases.notes: This is not the actual פסוק. It is the plain wording the תורה could have used instead.

phrases.english: Why does it say “to the court”?
Learn from it that it is for the count.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אֵין דּוֹרְשִׁין תְּחִילּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 5
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that רבי יאשיה holds דורשין תחילות as a general rule
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יאשיה counts the first mention only because the תורה used the unusual word אלהים instead of שופט
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Everyone agrees that first mentions are not counted. In this case the unusual wording makes the first mention countable for רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן hold אין דורשין תחילות. רבי יאשיה counts the first אלהים only because the תורה chose that word over 'the judge'.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: The תורה just used everyday language
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן explains that the first אלהים is simply normal speech for 'go to court,' so it does not signal an extra judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does רבי יונתן deal with this? He says the תורה used everyday language, the way people say: 'Whoever has a case should go to the judge.'
steps.whatsHappening: In step 6 the גמרא said the תורה could have written 'the judge' instead of אלהים. Now it shows why רבי יונתן is not convinced: people talk this way all the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יאשיה, choosing the word אלהים is a hint that this mention should also be counted. רבי יונתן says it is just the ordinary way of saying 'go to court.' Since it is normal wording, it hints at nothing, and he still counts only two mentions.

keyTerms.meaning: everyday language, the normal way people talk

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yonatan? (How does he explain this?)
phrases.notes: The גמרא leaves the question unspoken: why doesn't the word אלהים bother him the way it bothers רבי יאשיה?

phrases.english: The verse used everyday language,
as people say:
Whoever has a case
should go to the judge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how רבי יונתן answers the reason given in step 6 for counting the first אלהים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The wording is explained as ordinary speech, so it carries no extra teaching.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The unusual choice of אלהים over 'the judge' might seem to signal a third judge.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי יונתן, אלהים here is common speech for 'the court,' so it is not counted.

steps.title: Does רבי יאשיה reject the rule that a court must have an odd number?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה needed all three mentions to reach three judges, which suggests he does not require an odd-numbered court. A ברייתא says the תורה does require one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יאשיה not accept that a court must 'lean,' meaning it must have an odd number of judges? But a ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר the son of רבי יוסי הגלילי says, what does the פסוק 'to lean after the majority' teach? The תורה is saying: make yourself a court that can lean, one with an odd number of judges.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks רבי יאשיה. His method suggests he does not think a court must have an odd number, yet a ברייתא says the תורה demands it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן reached three by counting two and adding one so the court would be odd. If רבי יאשיה also held this rule, two mentions would already give him three, and he would not need to count the third. Since he does count it, it seems he rejects the rule, which goes against the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: a court that can 'lean' to one side, meaning one with an odd number of judges so there is always a majority
what does the verse come to teach?

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יאשיה never says outright that he rejects an odd-numbered court. The גמרא is drawing this from his method: if he held the rule, he would not have needed the third mention of אלהים.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoshiya,
does he not hold of a court that leans (an odd number of judges)?
phrases.notes: If he held this rule, two mentions plus one added judge would already make three, like רבי יונתן.

phrases.english: But it was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי אוֹמֵר,
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, says:
What does the verse come to teach
"to lean after the majority to turn [judgment]"?
phrases.notes: שמות 23:2

phrases.english: The Torah is saying:
Make for yourself a court that can lean (to a majority).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה לֵית לֵיהּ בֵּית דִּין נוֹטֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבי יונתן, the גמרא turns to challenge רבי יאשיה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יאשיה's method of counting all three mentions of אלהים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Needing a third mention implies he rejects the odd-number rule, but a ברייתא derives that rule from a פסוק.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה follows רבי יהודה, who allows a court of seventy
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה holds like רבי יהודה, who says the Great סנהדרין has seventy judges, so an even-numbered court is possible.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds like רבי יהודה, who says seventy. As we learned in a משנה: the Great סנהדרין had seventy-one judges. רבי יהודה says: seventy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי יאשיה really does not require an odd number, and he has support: רבי יהודה, who says the Great סנהדרין has seventy judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seventy is an even number. So רבי יהודה clearly does not hold that every court must be odd. רבי יאשיה follows him and disagrees with the ברייתא of רבי אליעזר בנו של רבי יוסי הגלילי.

keyTerms.meaning: he holds like (follows the opinion of)
the Great סנהדרין, the highest court

phrases.english: He holds like Rabbi Yehuda,
who says: seventy.
As we learned in a משנה:

phrases.aramaic: סַנְהֶדְרִי גְּדוֹלָה הָיְתָה שֶׁל שִׁבְעִים וְאֶחָד,
phrases.english: The Great Sanhedrin had seventy-one judges;
Rabbi Yehuda says: seventy.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּאָמַר: שִׁבְעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 by giving רבי יאשיה a תנא who allows an even-numbered court.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Matches the opinion to another תנא who shares it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone seemed to require a court with an odd number of judges.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יאשיה follows רבי יהודה, who allows a court of seventy, an even number.

steps.title: Maybe רבי יהודה's seventy applies only to the Great סנהדרין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: רבי יהודה may allow seventy only for the Great סנהדרין, because פסוקים spell it out, and not for other courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that you heard רבי יהודה say this about the Great סנהדרין, where פסוקים are written about it. Did you hear him say it about the other courts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave. רבי יהודה's ruling may be a special case that cannot be stretched to ordinary courts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Great סנהדרין's size comes straight from פסוקים, so seventy may be an exception set by the verses. That does not show רבי יהודה would allow an even number in a regular court. So the support for רבי יאשיה is now in doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: say that you heard him (say this only in one case)
did you hear him say it? (implying: no)

phrases.english: Say that you heard Rabbi Yehuda say this
about the Great Sanhedrin,
where verses are written about it.
phrases.notes: He means the פסוקים that describe how the Great סנהדרין is made up, so its number is set by the verses.

phrases.english: About the other courts,
did you hear him say it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימַר דְּשָׁמְעַתְּ לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּסַנְהֶדְרִי גְּדוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 9 by limiting רבי יהודה's view to one special court.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יאשיה can rely on רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה's seventy may be an exception set by the פסוקים about the Great סנהדרין, so it proves nothing about ordinary courts.

steps.title: Blocking the idea that רבי יהודה treats all courts the same
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off a possible defense, that רבי יהודה allows even-numbered courts everywhere, by quoting a משנה where רבי יהודה requires five judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say there is no difference between the Great סנהדרין and other courts: we learned in a משנה that סמיכת זקנים and עריפת עגלה need three judges, according to רבי שמעון, and רבי יהודה says five.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing its challenge from Step 10. It quotes a משנה to set up a proof, which it completes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might defend the answer of Step 9 by saying רבי יהודה allows even-numbered courts everywhere. The גמרא answers by pointing to a case where רבי יהודה requires five judges. Why five and not four is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say: the גמרא is blocking a possible answer before it is given
The elders leaning their hands on the communal bull offering
Breaking the neck of the calf when a murder victim is found and the killer is unknown

phrases.english: And if you would say: there is no difference,
phrases.notes: He means: maybe רבי יהודה lets every court, not just the Great סנהדרין, have an even number of judges.

phrases.english: but didn't we learn in a משנה:
The laying of hands by the elders and the breaking of the calf's neck are done with three judges,
these are the words of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehuda says: with five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge of Step 10 by blocking a possible defense.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible claim that רבי יהודה allows even-numbered courts in all courts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה requires five judges for סמיכה, which points to an odd-number rule in ordinary courts.

steps.title: Why רבי יהודה requires five judges
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי יהודה's reasoning: the פסוק gives four, and a fifth is added because a court cannot be evenly split, which proves he requires odd courts outside the Great סנהדרין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we said: what is רבי יהודה's reason? 'And they shall lay' means two, 'elders' means two, and a court cannot be evenly balanced, so we add one more, making five.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof by giving the reason for רבי יהודה's 'five'. It shows that רבי יהודה himself uses the rule that a court cannot be even.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural words in the פסוק only give four judges. רבי יהודה adds a fifth only because of the rule אין בית דין שקול. So רבי יהודה does hold that rule in ordinary courts, and the defense 'there is no difference' fails.

keyTerms.meaning: A court may not be evenly balanced, meaning it must have an odd number

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה allows an even number, seventy, only for the Great סנהדרין. In other courts he requires an odd number.

phrases.english: And we said: what is the reason of Rabbi Yehuda?
"And they shall lay their hands" means two,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 4:15

phrases.english: "elders" means another two,
and a court cannot be evenly balanced,
so we add one more to them,
so here there are five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning that turns the משנה of Step 11 into a proof.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהודה holds the rule of אין בית דין שקול in ordinary courts.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The explanation of רבי יהודה's view on סמיכת זקנים: four from the פסוק plus one.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה goes further than רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יאשיה builds on רבי יהודה but goes further, allowing even-numbered courts in all courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יאשיה goes further than רבי יהודה. רבי יהודה rejects the odd-number rule only for the Great סנהדרין and accepts it in other courts, while רבי יאשיה rejects it in other courts too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that רבי יהודה requires odd courts in ordinary cases. It answers that רבי יאשיה simply takes a stronger position than רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer of Step 9 did not mean רבי יאשיה is exactly like רבי יהודה. It means רבי יהודה shows that the odd-number rule is not absolute, and רבי יאשיה extends that to all courts.

keyTerms.meaning: Other courts, below the Great סנהדרין

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoshiya goes further than Rabbi Yehuda,
because whereas Rabbi Yehuda,
it is only for the Great Sanhedrin that he does not hold the rule,
phrases.notes: 'The rule' means that a court must have an odd number of judges.

phrases.aramaic: הָא בִּשְׁאָר בֵּי דִינָא אִית לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: but in other courts he does hold it.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה בִּשְׁאָר בֵּי דִינָא נָמֵי לֵית לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoshiya does not hold it in other courts either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 10-12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Refines the comparison: רבי יאשיה is not identical to רבי יהודה but goes further than him.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יאשיה needs to match רבי יהודה exactly, and רבי יהודה requires odd courts in ordinary cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יאשיה rejects the odd-number rule even in ordinary courts, going beyond רבי יהודה.

steps.title: What does רבי יאשיה do with the פסוק of majority rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יאשיה explains the פסוק 'לנטות', which is the source for needing an odd-numbered court.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, what does he do with this word 'to incline'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי יאשיה does with the פסוק that teaches majority rule. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The odd-number rule comes from this פסוק. If רבי יאשיה rejects the rule, the גמרא wants to know what the פסוק teaches according to him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'To incline', from the פסוק about following the majority
What does he do with it, meaning how does he use this source

phrases.english: But then, this word "to incline"
phrases.notes: שמות 23:2. This is the פסוק used to teach that a court must have an odd number.

phrases.english: what does he do with it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on Step 13 by asking about the source of the odd-number rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How רבי יאשיה reads the פסוק 'לנטות' if he rejects the odd-number rule.

steps.title: He applies it to capital cases
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה applies the פסוק of 'לנטות' to דיני נפשות, so the odd-number rule holds there.
steps.simpleTranslation: He applies it to capital cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יאשיה applies the פסוק only to capital cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So רבי יאשיה does accept the odd-number rule, but only in דיני נפשות. In ordinary money cases he does not require it.

keyTerms.meaning: He applies it to, he sets it in
Capital cases, cases of life and death

phrases.english: He applies it to capital cases.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'לנטות' teaches the odd-number rule for דיני נפשות only.

steps.title: Does the majority-vote משנה go against רבי יאשיה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: a משנה rules by a two-to-one majority in money cases, which seems to need an odd court. Does that mean the משנה disagrees with רבי יאשיה?
steps.simpleTranslation: But in money cases, not? What about the משנה: if two say not liable and one says liable, he is not liable; if two say liable and one says not liable, he is liable. Shall we say it is not like רבי יאשיה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the claim that רבי יאשיה does not require odd courts in money cases. It quotes a משנה that decides money cases by majority vote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה assumes a three-judge money case decided by majority, two against one. The גמרא suggests that רבי יאשיה, who does not use the majority פסוק for money cases, might disagree with this משנה. It is uncomfortable to say that a basic משנה goes against him.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? A suggestion the גמרא is testing

phrases.english: But in money cases he does not hold it?
But what about that which we learned in a משנה:
If two judges say he is not liable
and one says he is liable, he is not liable;
if two say he is liable
and one says he is not liable, he is liable.
Shall we say this is not like Rabbi Yoshiya?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל בְּדִינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת – לָא? אֶלָּא הָא דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of Step 15 that רבי יאשיה limits the odd-number rule to דיני נפשות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יאשיה does not require an odd-numbered court in money cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה decides money cases by a two-to-one majority, which seems to assume the majority rule applies there too.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה learns majority rule for money cases from capital cases
steps.stepSummary: The משנה can follow רבי יאשיה, because he learns majority rule for money cases through a קל וחומר from דיני נפשות.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say the משנה follows רבי יאשיה. He learns majority rule through a קל וחומר from capital cases: if in strict capital cases the תורה says 'follow the majority,' then in money cases, all the more so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 16. The משנה's two-to-one majority rule does not have to disagree with רבי יאשיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה does not require an odd-numbered court for money cases, but he still accepts majority rule there. He learns it from capital cases: if majority rules even where life is at stake, it surely rules in money matters. So an even court is allowed, and when the judges disagree, the majority still decides.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say (it follows this opinion)
A logical argument: if it is true in the strict case, it is surely true in the lighter case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up two separate ideas. 'The court must have an odd number' and 'the majority decides' are not the same thing. רבי יאשיה rejects the first for money cases but accepts the second.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rabbi Yoshiya;

phrases.aramaic: מַיְיתֵי לַהּ בְּקַל וָחוֹמֶר מִדִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת:
phrases.english: he derives it through a kal vachomer from capital cases:
If in capital cases, which are strict,
the Merciful One said 'Go after the majority,'
phrases.notes: This is the idea of the פסוק 'אחרי רבים להטות' (שמות 23:2).

phrases.english: then in money cases, is it not all the more so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Majority rule in money cases needs an odd court, so the משנה must disagree with רבי יאשיה
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יאשיה gets majority rule from a קל וחומר, so the משנה fits his view

steps.title: רבי says money cases need five judges
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the חכמים say money cases are judged by three; רבי says by five, so that the verdict is reached by three.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: money cases are judged by three. רבי says: by five, so that the verdict is decided by three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא. It brings a מחלוקת about how many judges sit on a money case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים say three judges are enough. רבי says five, and gives a reason: the verdict must be decided by three. The next steps will work out what that reason means.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Money cases are judged by three;
Rebbi says: by five,
so that the verdict will be decided by three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the size of the court for money cases
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חכמים: three judges; רבי: five judges, so that the verdict is reached by three

steps.title: Can't a three-judge court decide by two?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי's wording: even a court of three can reach a verdict by a majority of two.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that with three judges, a verdict cannot be decided by two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רבי's reason. A court of three can already decide with a two-to-one majority, so why say you need five 'so that three decide'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken literally, רבי's reason sounds like a court of three could never reach a verdict unless all three agree. But we know majority rules, so two out of three is enough. The גמרא wants to know what רבי really means.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (a challenging question)

phrases.english: Is that to say that with three,
the verdict is not decided by two?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ בִּתְלָתָא מִי לָא גָּמַר דִינָא בִּתְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in Step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's reason 'so that the verdict is decided by three'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A three-judge court can rule by a two-to-one majority, so you do not need five judges to reach a verdict

steps.title: רבי means the verdict itself needs three
steps.stepSummary: רבי means that the judges who form the majority must themselves number three.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he means: because a verdict must be decided by three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי's words. He is not saying three judges can't reach a verdict. He is saying the majority that decides the case must itself be three judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי, the תורה's number 'three' is the number of judges who must agree on the verdict. With five judges, a three-to-two vote gives a majority of three. With only three judges, a two-to-one vote leaves just two on the deciding side.

phrases.english: This is what he means:
because a verdict must be decided by three.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁגְּמַר דִּין בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי holds a court of three cannot reach a verdict by two
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי holds the deciding majority itself must be three judges, so you need five

steps.title: For רבי, the תורה's three refers to the verdict
steps.stepSummary: From this we see that רבי reads the three judges in the תורה as the number needed to decide the verdict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Evidently he holds: when the three are written in the תורה, they are written about the final verdict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion about how רבי reads the תורה. This sets up רבי אבהו's attack in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה mentions 'אלהים' three times in the section about money cases, and from this we learn that three judges are needed. רבי understands that these three must be the deciding majority, not just the judges sitting on the court. This is the exact point רבי אבהו will challenge.

phrases.english: Evidently he holds:
when the three are written,
phrases.notes: This refers to the three times 'אלהים' (judges) appears in the money-case section of שמות 22.

phrases.english: they are written about the final verdict.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא קָסָבַר: תְּלָתָא כִּי כְּתִיבִי – בִּגְמַר דִינָא כְּתִיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the underlying principle from the explanation in Step 20
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For רבי, the תורה's number of judges is the number needed to decide the verdict

steps.title: רבי אבהו: then the סנהדרין would need 141 judges
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו mocks רבי's logic: it would mean the Great סנהדרין needs 141 judges and the small one needs 45.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו mocked this: If so, the Great סנהדרין should need 141 judges, so that the verdict is decided by 71! And the small סנהדרין should need 45, so that the verdict is decided by 23!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו attacks רבי's principle by showing it leads to impossible results. Everyone knows the סנהדרין has 71 judges and the small סנהדרין has 23.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the תורה's number always means 'the deciding majority,' then the 71 must all be on the winning side. That needs a court of 141, so 71 can outvote 70. The same goes for the small court: 23 needs a court of 45, so 23 can outvote 22. Since these numbers are clearly wrong, the principle must be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (introduces an absurd result)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu mocked it:
But if so,
the Great Sanhedrin should need
one hundred forty-one,
phrases.notes: With 141 judges, a vote of 71 against 70 gives a winning side of exactly 71.

phrases.english: so that the verdict will be decided by seventy-one?

phrases.aramaic: וּתְהֵא סַנְהֶדְרִי קְטַנָּה צְרִיכָה אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה,
phrases.english: And the small Sanhedrin should need forty-five,
so that the verdict will be decided by twenty-three?

steps.triggerLanguage: מְגַדֵּף בַּהּ רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the principle drawn in Step 21
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's principle that the תורה's number of judges means the deciding majority
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Applied to 71 and 23, it would require courts of 141 and 45, which is clearly not the law

steps.title: The תורה's numbers count the judges on the court
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו explains that each number in the פסוקים counts the judges from when the court is formed, not the size of the majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the Merciful One said 'Gather to Me seventy men,' meaning from the time of gathering there must be seventy. 'And the congregation shall judge... and the congregation shall save' also means from the time the congregation judges. So too, 'the owner of the house shall come near to the judges' means from the time of coming near there must be three.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives the right way to read the פסוקים. Each number tells us how many judges sit on the court, not how many must vote together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'gather,' 'judge,' and 'come near' all describe the moment the court is set up and the case begins. So each number is the size of the court that sits, not the size of the majority. This shows that 'so that three decide the verdict' cannot be the reason for רבי's five. The next step gives a different reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The judging by the congregation (the 23-judge court)

steps.whatToRemember: The numbers 71, 23, and 3 are the sizes of the courts. They are not the number of judges who must agree. This knocks out the explanation that רבי needs five so that three decide the verdict, but רבי's ruling of five still stands. The next step gives it a new source.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule for every court: the תורה fixes how many judges sit, and within that court a simple majority decides.

phrases.english: Rather, 'Gather to Me seventy men,'
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:16

phrases.english: the Merciful One said,
meaning from the time of gathering there must be seventy.
'And the congregation shall judge... and the congregation shall save' also,
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:24–25. This is the source for the 23-judge court.

phrases.english: means from the time the congregation judges.
So too:
'The owner of the house shall come near to the judges,'
phrases.notes: שמות 22:7. Here 'אלהים' means the judges.

phrases.english: means from the time of coming near there must be three.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא ״אֶסְפָה לִּי שִׁבְעִים אִישׁ״ אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי אבהו's attack by giving the correct reading of the פסוקים
steps.raayaObject: The numbers in the פסוקים count the judges on the court, not the majority

steps.title: A new source for רבי: the plural word means two judges
steps.stepSummary: After rejecting the earlier explanation, the גמרא offers a new reason for רבי: the plural verb ירשיען shows that the אלהים mentioned with it means two judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is רבי's reason: "Whom the judges shall condemn" is written in the plural, so it means two judges.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the explanation that רבי אבהו attacked and starts building a new explanation for רבי's five judges. This first step sets up the rest of the new explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old approach treated the numbers as the size of the majority, and that led to an absurd result. The new approach looks at the grammar of the פסוק instead. The verb ירשיען is plural, so the judges it describes must be at least two.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. The גמרא is dropping the previous idea and offering a new one.
They shall condemn. The verb is plural.

phrases.english: Rather, this is the reasoning of Rabbi:
"Whom the judges shall condemn" means two.
phrases.notes: שמות 22:8

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation that רבי אבהו rejected in steps 22-23 with a new reading of the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacement explanation based on the plural grammar of the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי's reason was that the three judges written in the תורה must be the deciding majority. Applied to the סנהדרין, that led to the absurd numbers 141 and 45.
steps.terutzMaskana: The plural verb ירשיען itself shows that the judges it refers to are two.

steps.title: Comparing the two mentions of אלהים gives two more judges
steps.stepSummary: The word אלהים appears both below and above. Since the one below means two judges, the one above also means two.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word "judges" is said below, and "judges" is said above. Just as below it means two, so too above it means two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects the two places where the word אלהים appears. This lets the "two judges" from the plural word carry over to the other mention as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the lower אלהים has a plural verb attached to it. Because the same word appears in both places, whatever is true of one is applied to the other. The result is 2 + 2, which means four judges so far.

keyTerms.meaning: Below, meaning later in the פסוק
Above, meaning earlier in the פסוק
Just as ... so too. This is the standard way of comparing two cases.

phrases.english: It is said "judges" below
phrases.notes: "Below" is the אלהים next to ירשיען, which we just learned means two. "Above" is the earlier mention of אלהים.

phrases.english: and it is said "judges" above.
Just as below it means two,
so too above it means two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the "two" from step 24 and extends it to the other mention of אלהים.
steps.raayaObject: That the upper mention of אלהים also means two judges, which gives four judges in total
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same word אלהים appears both below and above in the פסוק, and the lower one is shown to be plural by ירשיען.

steps.title: No even-numbered court, so one is added to make five
steps.stepSummary: Since a court cannot be evenly split, one judge is added to the four, which gives רבי's five judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a court may not have an even number of judges, so they add one more to them. That gives five here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the new explanation. It adds one judge to the four so that the court cannot end in a tie, and that reaches רבי's number of five.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים themselves only give four judges. The extra judge comes from a general rule, not from the פסוק: a court must have an odd number of judges so it can always reach a decision. 4 + 1 = 5 matches רבי's opinion, and this explanation avoids the problem רבי אבהו raised.

keyTerms.meaning: Evenly balanced, meaning an even number of judges that could end in a tie

steps.whatToRemember: According to this explanation, רבי's five judges come from 2 (the plural ירשיען) + 2 (comparing the two mentions of אלהים) + 1 (because a court cannot have an even number of judges).

phrases.english: And a court may not be even-numbered,
so they add one more to them.
So there are five here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the count from four to five by applying the rule that a court cannot have an even number of judges.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי's requirement of five judges comes from four judges learned from the פסוקים plus one more, because a court may not have an even number of judges.
